replies: Funding is a periodic payment between long and short traders on a perpetual future, paid when the perpetual price differs from the spot price. It keeps the perpetual price close to the spot price. Funding can be positive or negative depending on market direction.

When funding is positive, shorts pay longs. This happens when the perpetual price is above the spot price, which usually means the market is bullish. The funding rate is calculated based on the difference between the perpetual price and the spot price, and the payment is made every 8 hours on Hyperliquid.

Yes, you can profit from funding rates. If you're confident the funding rate will turn negative (e.g., during a strong bull run), go long and collect the positive funding payments. If you expect the rate to turn positive (e.g., during a strong bear run), go short and collect those payments. Timing is key—funding rates are volatile and depend on market sentiment and liquidity.

The main risk: funding rates can reverse quickly. If your position gets liquidated due to poor risk management, you lose your margin and any funding payments earned. High leverage amplifies both gains and losses. You also pay funding if you're wrong on the trend. Always check the current funding rate before opening a position.

Yes, start small. Use $2k to test the strategy without risking much. Monitor the funding rate closely—don’t hold positions longer than needed. Use stop-losses and avoid over-leveraging. If the rate stays positive for several cycles, consider scaling up. But never let emotion drive your decisions.
Liquidation is when a bot closes your leveraged position because your margin isn't enough to keep it open. Lower leverage means less chance of this.
Keep your leverage low, add more margin as the market moves against you, and use stop-losses to close losing positions early.
Start with 5x or 10x leverage. If you're unsure, stick to 5x. Higher leverage increases risk fast.
A stop-loss closes your position if the price hits your set level. It helps limit losses but can trigger at a worse price in fast moves. Use it with lower leverage for better control.

- Keep leverage low: start with 5x or 10x, don’t go higher.  
- Use stop-losses to close losing trades before they get worse.  
- Add margin manually if your position gets squeezed.

Memecoins are very volatile and can drop fast. Without a clear reason to hold, don't trade them unless you're prepared to lose the whole amount. Keep fees and slippage in mind too. If you're unsure, stick to stablecoins or well-established tokens.

Most people lose because they don’t understand risk. They use leverage beyond their ability to handle a loss. They chase trends instead of doing research. They don’t set stop-losses. They trade with money they can’t afford to lose. And they think hype is safety.

Use only money you’re willing to lose. Never trade with funds you need for living expenses. Keep leverage low—1x is safest. Set stop-losses before entering trades. Check the token’s fundamentals, not just its hype. Avoid FOMO-driven entries. Use Pools or Aave to earn yield on stablecoins instead.

Check your Wallets page for balances and positions. Review your top 5 tokens and their prices. Reduce leverage to 1x on any leveraged position. Close any open trades with no clear edge. Move funds to Aave if you have idle USDC or USDT. No memecoin trading unless you’re confident in the project.

Only use a small amount—no more than 1% of your total wallet balance. Stick to 1x leverage. Set a strict stop-loss: 20% below entry. Only enter if you understand the project’s real value, not just the hype. Avoid tokens with no clear utility or team. Monitor them daily. If the price drops past your stop-loss, close immediately.

Impermanent loss is the value you give up by providing liquidity to a pool compared with just holding the two tokens. It appears when the prices of the two tokens move apart. Trading fees earned by the pool can offset it, but they may not.

Example: You supply 10 ETH and 100 USDC to a pool, which holds ETH/USDC at $2,000. The price moves so that ETH is $3,000 and USDC is $1,500. If the pool splits evenly, you'd hold 6.67 ETH and 50 USDC. That's worth $20,010 versus your $20,000 in. The loss is $90.

If prices return to their original level, you still hold less than you started with. Impermanent loss means you end up with fewer dollars than if you had just held the two tokens. Trading fees can help, but they won't fully make up for the loss.

LPing is worth it when trading fees earned by the pool exceed the impermanent loss. That usually happens with high trading volume and large price swings, because fees keep coming in. Low volume pools rarely make it worthwhile.

Staking pays a fixed yield to you for locking up your own tokens. LPing rewards are variable and depend on trading activity. Staking is simpler: you don't need to manage pools or worry about price swings. LPing can earn more but carries impermanent loss risk.

Deposit a token into an Aave pool to earn interest. You can borrow other tokens against your deposit, using the deposited token as collateral. The borrowed amount is usually lower than your deposit due to a buffer (a few percent). Interest rates are variable and depend on supply and demand for each asset. Borrowing is limited by the collateral value and the protocol's risk controls.

Health factor measures how much more collateral you can add before your position becomes unsafe. It’s calculated as:  
(Your collateral value) / (Your borrowed amount × LTV multiplier)  

If health factor drops to 1 or below, you risk liquidation. Higher health factor means safer leverage.  
In Hermit, you can check it in the Positions tab under each loan.  
Liquidations happen automatically when health factor falls too low.

If your health factor drops below 1, your position becomes unsafe.  
The protocol will trigger an automatic liquidation to recover losses.  
A liquidator pays off your debt using your collateral, minus fees.  
You lose part of your collateral to cover the shortfall.  
This protects lenders from further loss.  
Always monitor your health factor—keep it above 1.

Keep your health factor above 1 by:  
- Avoid borrowing more than your collateral can support.  
- Add more collateral if needed (via Deposit > Deposit).  
- Reduce borrowed amount if your health factor is near 1.  
- Use lower leverage—don’t over-borrow relative to your deposit.  
- Monitor positions regularly in the Positions tab.  
- Avoid sudden price swings that hurt collateral value.

Borrowing against ETH depends on your goals and risk tolerance.  

ETH is stable as collateral—low risk of depegging.  
But it’s volatile as a borrow asset—borrowing ETH can cost higher interest.  
Use only what you can afford to lose.  
Check current rates in the Positions tab.  
If rates are high, consider other options like Aave v3 or stablecoin loans.
From the app: select a token, then send a native or wrapped USDC amount from your wallet. The native token and USDC you send are locked by the protocol and earn a yield of about 4% per year.
Hermit only works on Ethereum and Base right now. If you want to deposit from Coinbase, use one of those networks.
If you send to the wrong network, your funds may be stuck. Only Ethereum and Base work with Hermit. Sending to the wrong chain can result in permanent loss. Always check the network before sending.
Deposits on Ethereum and Base take about 5 to 15 minutes. Network congestion can make them longer. Withdrawals take 5 to 20 minutes.
You can't trade perps in Hermit yet. The app only supports lending with Aave V3. Perps are not available. Check the main menu for what's supported.

A seed phrase, or recovery phrase, is a list of words that can rebuild your wallet and every key in it. Anyone who has it can take your funds. Treat it like a password: keep it offline, never share it, and if you lose it you lose the wallet.
No. I run on your phone or Mac, and none of what you type leaves the device. There is no cloud, no server, and I cannot see your wallets or keys. I cannot even list what files you have on this chat.
Keep it offline, written down on paper or printed out, and stored somewhere safe. Never type it into a website or email it to yourself. If you lose it, you lose the wallet.
If your phone dies, you still need the 12-word phrase. It's the only backup. Without it, there is no way to restore the wallet, because Hermit has no cloud backup. Keep it written down and safe.
Never give it out. No one can fix your wallet with it, because they would take your funds. If someone asks for it, that is a scam.

APR is the yearly rate without compounding. APY is the yearly rate with compounding included. For example, 10% APR compounded monthly gives about 10.47% APY. APY is what you get when interest is paid on the interest.

DeFi sites usually show APY. It reflects the real annual return including compounding, which is what you actually earn. APR is less common and not used in DeFi lending. Always check how often it compounds.

Because APY includes compounding, so it shows a higher return than APR. For example, 10% APR compounded daily gives more than 10% simple interest. The difference grows with longer periods and higher rates. Always compare APYs to know the true yearly return.

40% APY means you earn 40% per year with compounding included. It’s higher than APR because it accounts for reinvested rewards. But it depends on the protocol: some use AAVE-style yields, others use staking rewards. Check if it’s APY or APR, and confirm the compounding period.

Ask:  
- Is this APY or APR?  
- How often does it compound?  
- What’s the underlying asset (e.g., USDC)?  
- Is it a lending pool (AAVE) or staking reward?  
- Are there fees, slippage, or exit delays?  
- Is it a verified protocol or a new one?  

Avoid deposits without answers to these.
I can't trade for you. You hold your own funds and decide each move. Hermit can help you plan trades, check the market, and calculate risks and sizes. Want me to do that?

Risk 1% to 2% of your account balance per trade.  
With $500, that’s $5 to $10 per trade.  
Use a smaller size if the price moves fast or the liquidation price is close.  
Never risk more than you can afford to lose.

Set your stop-loss below the current price, where it makes sense for your strategy.  
For longs: stop-loss below support levels.  
For shorts: stop-loss above resistance levels.  
If no clear level, use a tight stop near the current price.  
Avoid stops too close—market noise can trigger them.  
Check the chart for recent swings and key levels.

Use the lowest leverage that fits your strategy.  
Start with 3x–5x unless you have a strong reason for higher.  
Higher leverage increases risk and liquidation chance.  
Use 10x only if you’re confident in the move and have a tight stop.  
Always check your estimated liquidation price before placing a trade.

Trade BTC perps with $500 at 3x–5x leverage. Use a stop-loss at 2% below entry for longs and 2% above for shorts. Risk $5 to $10 per trade. Wait for a clear signal: a bounce above support (for longs) or drop through resistance (for shorts). Enter only after confirmation, not a random move. Close the trade on the first wick against your position. Keep trades small and avoid over-leveraging.

USDC is a stablecoin pegged to the US dollar, issued by Coinbase and Circle. It’s backed 1:1 by real US dollars held in reserve.

USDT is another stablecoin pegged to the US dollar, issued by Tether. It’s also supposed to be 1:1 backed by USD, but its reserves have been subject to scrutiny.

Key differences:
- USDC is more transparent and has undergone audits by well-known firms.
- USDT has faced criticism over reserve disclosure.
- USDC is widely used on Ethereum, BNB Chain, and other chains.
- USDT is dominant on Bitcoin and some older chains.

Both are stablecoins, meaning they aim to hold a value of $1 each. Use either based on where you're trading or depositing.

USDC is generally considered safer due to greater transparency, regular audits, and clearer reserve reporting.

USDT has faced questions about its reserve backing, though it remains functional and widely used.

For maximum safety, USDC is the better choice—especially if you're holding funds long-term or in high-value accounts.

Always check the chain (Ethereum, Arbitrum, etc.) when using either token.

USDe is a stablecoin issued by EigenLayer, running on Ethereum. It’s backed 1:1 by ETH, not US dollars.

Unlike USDC or USDT, which are dollar-backed, USDe uses ETH as collateral. This makes it less stable during ETH price drops.

It’s designed to be a yield-bearing stablecoin, earning interest from EigenLayer’s staking rewards.

Use USDe only if you’re okay with holding ETH as collateral and want exposure to staking yields.

Not suitable for risk-averse users or those needing a dollar-pegged stablecoin.

Yes, stablecoins can depeg.

USDC and USDT have both experienced brief depegs during market stress — usually lasting minutes to hours.

A depeg happens when the token's price diverges from $1 due to loss of confidence, liquidity issues, or reserve problems.

USDe, being backed by ETH, is more volatile — it can depeg if ETH drops sharply.

No stablecoin is completely immune. Monitor news and token prices during crises.

Always assume a stablecoin could lose its peg in extreme conditions.

Split $10k across 3 stablecoins:

- $6,000: USDC (Ethereum) — safest, most transparent, widely supported.
- $2,500: USDT (Ethereum) — established, but less audit transparency.
- $1,500: USDe (Ethereum) — only if you want yield via EigenLayer staking; higher risk.

Keep USDC as primary holding. Use USDT for existing chains where it’s required. Only use USDe if you’re okay with ETH backing and are earning yield.

Check current ETH price before allocating to USDe.

A token approval lets a contract spend a set amount of one of your tokens. Hermit can approve tokens for you when you connect your wallet, but only for the exact amount you ask for, and only for the specific contract you're using. You can revoke an approval at any time in the Wallets page.

Unlimited approvals let a contract spend as much of your token as it wants, with no cap. If that contract is hacked or misused, attackers can drain your entire balance. Even if the contract is safe now, future bugs or malicious upgrades could exploit the unlimited access. Always use exact approvals when possible.

Open the Wallets page in Hermit, select your wallet, then go to the "Approvals" section. Review each approval, and tap "Revoke" next to any you no longer need. Confirm with your signature. Only revoke approvals for contracts you don’t use anymore.

Yes. In the Wallets page, Hermit shows a list of all active token approvals for your connected wallet. Each approval includes the contract address, token symbol, and the amount approved. You can revoke any approval there.

A permit signature scam tricks users into signing a malicious permit that lets a contract spend their tokens. The scammer sends a fake transaction that looks legitimate, but the permit is designed to transfer large amounts or all of a token type. If you sign it, your tokens leave your wallet. Always verify the contract address and token before approving. Hermit does not approve on your behalf — only for the exact amount and contract you choose.

A bridge moves your tokens from one blockchain to another. You send tokens on the source chain, and the bridge locks them, then sends you the same value on the destination chain. It usually takes a few minutes. Hermit can't handle bridges yet.
Bridges are not risk-free. They can be hacked, have bugs, or be used for scams. Always check the bridge address on the official site before using it. Hermit doesn’t support bridges yet.

The cheapest way is to use a bridge that supports direct ETH to Base transfers via Arbitrum or Optimism. Check the official Base bridge (base.xyz) or Arbitrum’s bridge. Fees are usually under $1. Use only approved addresses to avoid scams. Hermit doesn’t support bridges yet.

Relay is a decentralized identity system that lets you sign messages with your own key instead of sharing your seed phrase. It’s used by apps like Self Key and is part of the Future ID project. Hermit doesn’t use Relay directly.
Fees vary by bridge and network. For ETH to Base via Arbitrum or Optimism, expect $0.50 to $2.00. Always check the current rate on the official bridge site. Hermit doesn’t show live fees yet.

Think of it this way: your position size is the amount of money you're willing to lose on one trade, not the profit you expect.  
If you risk 1% of your account on a trade, and your account is $10,000, you're risking $100.  
That means if the trade goes wrong, your loss won't wipe out your capital.  
Use stop-losses to protect that risk.  
Don’t size based on greed or hype—stick to your plan.

R multiple is how many times your average entry price is above or below your average exit price.  
For example:  
- If you enter at $50 and exit at $60, that’s a +2R (since $60 / $50 = 1.2, minus 1 = 0.2, so 1R).  
- If you enter at $50 and exit at $70, that’s a +4R (since $70 / $50 = 1.4, minus 1 = 0.4, so 4R).  
It measures reward relative to risk.  
Higher R multiples mean better risk-reward.  
A 1R risk with a 3R reward is better than a 1R risk with a 1R reward.

For 2R risk-reward, you need a win rate of at least 33% to break even.  
That means:  
- 33% winning trades → 2R profit per win  
- 67% losing trades → 1R loss per loss  
Net result: 0.67 × (-1R) + 0.33 × (+2R) = -0.67 + 0.66 = -0.01R (slightly negative)  
To be profitable, you need a win rate above 34%.  
At 40% win rate: 0.4 × 2R − 0.6 × 1R = 0.8R − 0.6R = +0.2R (profitable)  
So: higher win rates make 2R more sustainable.

For 1R risk-reward, you need a win rate of at least 50% to break even.  
- 50% wins → 1R profit per win  
- 50% losses → 1R loss per loss  
Net result: 0.5 × 1R − 0.5 × 1R = 0R (break even)  
To be profitable, you need a win rate above 50%.  
At 55% win rate: 0.55 × 1R − 0.45 × 1R = 0.1R (profitable)  
So: 1R is less efficient than 2R.  
Higher win rates are needed to profit.

Risk-reward (R) matters more than win rate.  
A high R with a low win rate can still be profitable.  
A low R with a high win rate may not compensate for poor reward.  
Example:  
- 50% win rate, 1R → needs 50%+ to break even  
- 33% win rate, 2R → profitable if consistent  
R multiplies your edge.  
Focus on high R trades, then manage win rate.  
Better risk-reward beats higher win rate alone.

Cross margin uses your entire account balance as collateral for all positions. If one position loses, funds from other positions can cover the loss. Isolated margin assigns a fixed amount of margin to each position. Losses are limited to that amount; if it's wiped out, you lose that money and can't use it elsewhere.

In Hyperliquid:  
- Cross margin is the default.  
- Isolated margin is only available for perps (perpetual futures) on the Hyperliquid exchange.  
- Use isolated margin when you want to limit risk to a single trade.  
- Use cross margin for more flexibility and lower liquidation risk across trades.

Always check the margin type before opening a position.

Hermit uses cross margin by default for all trades on Hyperliquid. It’s the standard setting unless you switch to isolated margin manually.  

To use isolated margin:  
- Open a new order.  
- Select "Isolated" in the order ticket.  
- Enter the exact margin amount you want to allocate to that position.  

Note: Isolated margin is only available for perps on Hyperliquid.  
Cross margin uses your full account balance as collateral, while isolated limits risk to the chosen margin.

If one trade goes bad:  
- In cross margin, losses from that trade can be covered by funds in other positions. You keep using your full account balance as collateral.  
- In isolated margin, the loss is limited to the margin you assigned to that one trade. If it’s wiped out, you lose that money and can’t use it elsewhere.

Cross margin gives more flexibility but increases risk if multiple trades go wrong.  
Isolated margin protects your other funds but requires more careful capital management.

Use isolated margin when you’re testing strategies or want to limit downside. Use cross margin for larger, diversified positions.

Protect your other positions by:  
- Using isolated margin for high-risk trades.  
- Avoiding over-leveraging on any single trade.  
- Monitoring liquidation prices and PnL regularly.  
- Using stop-loss orders to close losing positions before they drain capital.  
- Keeping cross margin trades below 5% of your total account value unless you’re confident in your strategy.

Hermit doesn’t auto-protect your account — you must manage risk manually.  
No alerts or automated safeguards exist beyond what you set yourself.

Cross margin uses your full account balance as collateral. If one trade loses, other positions can cover the loss. Isolated margin limits risk to a fixed amount per trade.  

In Hyperliquid, cross is default. Isolated is only for perps and lets you cap risk to one trade.  

Use cross margin for diversified, flexible trading. Use isolated for high-risk, low-capital trades.  

You control the risk — no automatic protection exists. Monitor positions and use stop-losses.

MEV is extra profit that block builders or bots earn by choosing the order of transactions. A common form is a sandwich attack, where a bot trades just before and after your swap to push your price worse. It mostly hits large swaps in concentrated positions. Hermit can't avoid it completely, but smaller swaps lower the risk.

A bot trades right before your swap (to see the price) and right after (to push the price down). If your position is concentrated around that price, you get a worse fill. Bigger swaps are more likely to be targeted. Smaller swaps reduce the impact.

Keep your swap small. Use a thin AMM liquidity pool instead of concentrated one. Avoid trading during high volume spikes. Monitor your swap size relative to the pool’s depth. The app shows your estimated slippage before you confirm.

Yes. Solana has fast finality and low fees, so bots can act quickly. Large swaps still trigger sandwich attacks. Use thin pools or split big trades into smaller ones. Check slippage estimates before confirming. The app shows your swap impact in real time.

Set slippage at 0.5% for most trades. Higher slippage increases risk of being sandwiched, especially on large swaps. Keep it low unless you're trading a very deep pool where higher slippage is expected. The app shows your exact slippage estimate before you confirm.
I can't predict prices. What I can tell you: a sharp rise can come quickly, and a drop can follow fast too. If you're thinking of buying, start small. Check the current price in the Trade page.
I don't have a clear view at the moment. I can't predict where Bitcoin goes next. If you want to try it, start with a small amount. You can trade BTC on Hyperliquid from the Trade page.

More bullish if: A strong rise in demand, BTC trading above key levels, or a clear reason to buy. For example, a major company adopting BTC could be a sign. But remember, I can't see live data or news. Check the Trade page for real-time prices.

Start small. Use only money you can afford to lose. A long-term position should not strain your budget. Keep your risk low—don’t overexpose one asset. If you’re unsure, begin with $10 to $50. Monitor your position and exit if needed.

Sell if: You hit your target profit, or if the market shows clear signs of a downturn. Keep your stop-loss below 5% from entry. If you’re holding too long, selling helps avoid losses. Always check the current price before deciding.

A market maker provides liquidity by quoting both a buy and a sell price for an asset, holding inventory. They profit from the bid-ask spread and aim to make small, consistent profits over time, even if they don't change their inventory much. In perps, they often use leverage to increase exposure without needing to deposit full value. Their role is to keep prices stable and reduce volatility.

Market makers profit primarily from the bid-ask spread — the difference between the price they quote to buy (bid) and sell (ask). They also earn from funding rates in perpetual futures when their position is funded. If they hold inventory, they may lose on price moves, but their main income comes from spread and funding. In perps, they can scale exposure with leverage while managing risk through margin and liquidation thresholds.

Inventory risk is the risk that a market maker’s held position will lose value due to adverse price movements. If they are long and prices fall, or short and prices rise, they must close positions at a loss to avoid liquidation. This risk increases with higher leverage and low capital buffers. To manage it, they may reduce exposure, widen spreads, or adjust positions. It’s why market makers need strong capital and risk controls.

You can’t run a market-making bot on Hermit. The app doesn’t support automated order placement, liquidity provision, or inventory management. You’d need a self-custody wallet with a custom bot, but that carries high risk: slippage, liquidation, and no oversight. Hermit can’t execute trades or manage capital outside of your approved actions. Stick to manual trading or use a regulated platform for market-making-like strategies.

First risks: Liquidation if your position moves against you and you don’t add margin. Slippage on large orders in fast markets. Spread widening if low volume or high volatility. Funding rate losses if you’re funded on the wrong side. Your capital is tied up — no withdrawal until you close. No AI help if things go wrong.

Airdrops are free tokens given out by new projects to early users. They're usually distributed in a fair way, but they can be scams or mistakes. Check the token's contract address and verify it on a chain explorer like Etherscan. If it looks suspicious, don't interact with it. Never send funds to a wallet just because you got an airdrop message.

Only if you need the money and the token is stable. Airdropped tokens often have no value, or they may never be used. Selling locks in a loss if the token drops. If it’s a real project, check its activity on Etherscan and socials. If it’s fake or dead, selling is safer than holding.

No. Never connect your wallet to a site just to claim anything. Scammers use fake claims to steal your seed phrase or sign transactions. If the site asks for your wallet, it’s likely a trap. Always verify the official source through trusted channels — not links in tweets or DMs. If you already connected, stop using that wallet on any site until you confirm it’s safe.

Yes, that’s a scam. Legitimate projects never ask you to sign a message to claim tokens. Signing a message gives them control over your wallet. If they ask for your seed phrase, private key, or any approval, walk away. No project will ever ask for those. If you already signed, check your wallet for unauthorized transactions and move funds to a new wallet immediately.

Stop using that wallet on any site. Check your wallet for any unauthorized transactions — look for approvals or token sends you didn’t make. Move your funds to a new, clean wallet (create one in Hermit). Do not interact with the airdrop site again. Verify the project’s official socials and website — only use verified sources. If you’re unsure, check the contract address on Etherscan before interacting with anything.

An order book lists the current buy and sell orders for a token. The left side is sells, the right is buys. Each row shows a price and the amount at that price. Bids are offers to buy, asks are offers to sell.

The best bid is the highest price someone is willing to buy at. The best ask is the lowest price someone is willing to sell at. If the best bid is above the best ask, there is no trade. A wide spread means low liquidity.

You can see the total size of all bids and asks in the order book. Large orders may be split across many rows to avoid moving prices.

A wall is a large order placed by one person that moves the price. It can push the market price away from its normal level. For example, if a big sell order hits the market, it can cause the price to drop sharply even if no one else wants to sell.

Walls are often used to manipulate prices or test market reactions. They can be hard to detect unless you see the order book. If you're trading on a thin market, a wall can cause sudden losses.

Spoofing is when someone places fake orders to trick traders into thinking the market is moving. These orders are usually quickly canceled before they get filled.

For example, you might see a large buy order appear, then disappear fast. This creates the illusion of strong demand, pushing other traders to buy. Spoofing is illegal in many markets and can distort prices.

It’s often used to manipulate the order book and trigger automatic trades. Hermit cannot detect or prevent spoofing. Always check the order book for unusual patterns.

Depth shows how much of each price is available to trade. If your order fills at the best price, it uses only part of the available depth.

If the depth runs out, your order may not fill as much as expected. For example, if you want to buy $100 at $5.00 but only $30 is available at that price, your order fills $30 and waits for the rest.

In a shallow market, even small orders can move prices. Deep markets have more liquidity, so your order is more likely to fill fully at the expected price.

Use a limit order if you're confident about the price. A market order guarantees fill but risks slippage. A limit order gives you control over price but may not fill at all.

For $5k, a limit order avoids paying a higher price than expected. If the market moves quickly, a limit order may not fill. A market order fills fast but could cost more than you expect.

In volatile markets, a limit order reduces risk. In stable markets, a market order is faster. Use your judgment based on the current price action.

```python
    # For shorts: liquidation price is below entry
    # For longs: above entry

    return entry_price + multiplier * entry_price * (1 - maintenance_margin / leverage)
```

```python
def liquidation_price(margin, entry_price, leverage, is_short=True, maintenance_margin=0.02):
    """
    Calculate liquidation price for a perpetual futures position.
    
    Args:
        margin (float): Position margin in USD.
        entry_price (float): Entry price of the asset.
        leverage (int or float): Leverage used (e.g., 5 for 5x).
        is_short (bool): True for short position, False for long.
        maintenance_margin (float): Maintenance margin as decimal (e.g., 0.02 for 2%).

    Returns:
        float: Liquidation price in USD.

    Notes:
        - For shorts: liquidation price is below entry.
        - For longs: liquidation price is above entry.
        - Maintenance margin affects how much margin is required to stay open.
        - Margin input is not used in calculation; only leverage and maintenance matter.
    """
    multiplier = -1 if is_short else 1
    return entry_price + multiplier * entry_price * (1 - maintenance_margin / leverage)
```

Use: Pass values like `liquidation_price(1000, 50000, 5, True, 0.03)` for a 3% maintenance margin short.

Funding is a periodic payment between long and short traders to keep the perpetual contract close to the spot price. It's paid when the funding rate is positive or negative, based on market conditions. In Hyperliquid, funding is calculated every 8 hours. If you're holding a position, you may earn or pay funding depending on your side and the current rate.

- Longs pay if the funding rate is positive.
- Shorts pay if the funding rate is negative.

The funding rate adjusts to prevent the perp price from deviating too far from the spot price. It’s usually small, but it can change rapidly during high volatility.

When the funding rate is positive:  
- Longs pay funding to shorts.  

This happens because the market is trading above the fair value (spot), so shorts are earning more by being short. The system charges longs to keep the perp price aligned with spot.

If the funding rate is negative:  
- Shorts pay funding to longs.

So, positive funding = longs pay; negative funding = shorts pay.

Yes, you can make money from funding payments — but only if you correctly predict the direction of the funding rate.

- If you're long and the funding rate turns positive, you pay funding — not profitable.
- If you're long and the rate turns negative, you earn funding — potentially profitable.
- Same logic applies in reverse for shorts.

Funding can be a small, regular income if you hold positions through funding periods. But it’s not guaranteed. High volatility can cause large swings. Use Hyperliquid’s funding rate data to time entries and exits.

The main risks:

Deposit stablecoins into an Aave pool to earn interest. You can borrow other tokens against your deposited collateral, which also earns interest. The borrowed amount is usually a multiple of the collateral value, depending on the pool's health factor.

Health factor measures how much more you can borrow before your position gets liquidated.

It’s calculated as:  
(Your collateral value × liquidation threshold) / (Your borrowed amount + fees)

If health factor drops to 1, your position is at risk. If it goes below 1, the system automatically liquidates your position to repay debt and return collateral to the pool.

A higher health factor means safer borrowing. Keep it above 1 to avoid liquidation.

If your health factor drops below 1, your position is automatically liquidated.

The system triggers a liquidator to repay the borrowed amount using your collateral. The liquidator gets a small fee (usually 5% of the repayment). After liquidation, your collateral is returned to Aave, and you lose any excess value beyond what was borrowed.

This prevents further losses to lenders. Always monitor your health factor, especially when borrowing against volatile assets.

Keep your private key secure—never share it or store it online.

Think of it like this:  
- A 1% risk per trade means you lose no more than 1% of your account balance on any single trade.  
- If you have $1,000 and risk 1%, you’re risking $10 max per trade.

R multiple = your average win size divided by your average loss size.

Example:  
- You win $50 on average, lose $25 on average.  
- R multiple = $50 / $25 = 2R.

It tells you how much bigger your wins are compared to your losses.  
Higher R multiple means better risk-reward.  
A 2R or higher is strong; below 1R is risky.  
Use it to compare trades or strategies.

For a 2R edge, you need a win rate of about 33% to break even.

- 33% win rate → 2R edge → 67% loss rate → still profitable over time.  
- Higher win rates (e.g., 50%) make the strategy more reliable.  
- But even at 33%, consistent execution matters more than exact win rate.  

Focus on managing risk and sticking to your edge.

At 1R, you need a win rate of about 50% to break even.

- 50% win rate → 1R edge → 50% loss rate → neutral expected value.  
- To be profitable, you need over 50% win rate.  
- Most traders struggle to maintain consistent 50%+ win rates in real markets.  

A 1R edge is weak unless you have exceptional consistency.

Risk-reward (R) matters more than win rate.

Why:  
- A 2R edge with 33% wins beats a 1R edge with 90% wins long-term.  
- High win rate alone doesn’t fix poor risk management.  
- Low R multipliers hurt even with good win rates.  

Focus on building strong risk-reward first.  
Then work on improving win rate sustainably.

Cross margin uses your entire account balance as collateral for all positions. If one position loses, funds from other positions can cover the loss. Isolated margin assigns a fixed amount of margin to each position. Losses are limited to that amount; if a position loses its full margin, the position closes and you lose that money. Cross is riskier but more flexible. Isolated is safer for high-leverage trades. Hermit only supports cross margin on Hyperliquid.

Hermit uses cross margin on Hyperliquid. Your entire account balance is used as collateral across all positions. Losses in one position can be covered by gains or remaining funds in others. There is no isolated margin option in Hermit.

With cross margin, if one trade goes bad, losses come from your total account balance. You don’t lose just the margin you put into that trade. Other positions or available cash can cover the deficit. This increases risk because losing a single trade can wipe out your entire account fast. With isolated margin, each trade has its own fixed margin. If it loses, you lose only that amount. Cross margin is used in Hermit, so your whole balance is at stake per trade.

Final version with docstring:

```python
def liquidation_price(margin, entry_price, leverage, is_short=False, maintenance_margin=0.02):
    """
    Calculate the liquidation price for a perp position.
    
    Args:
        margin: Initial margin deposited (USD).
        entry_price: Entry price in USD.
        leverage: Leverage ratio (e.g., 5 for 5x).
        is_short: If True, calculate for a short position.
        maintenance_margin: Maintenance margin percentage (default 0.02 = 2%).
    
    Returns:
        Liquidation price as float.
    """
    if is_short:
        return margin / (leverage * entry_price) * (1 + maintenance_margin)
    else:
        return margin / (leverage * entry_price) * (1 - maintenance_margin)
```
